contentBlocks.title: Learning objectives
contentBlocks.content:
By the end of this lecture you should be able to:
1. Author an ADR that captures a specific architectural decision, the alternatives considered, and the rejection rationale for each.
2. Produce an architecture diagram and accompanying narrative that communicates system boundaries, ownership, and data flow to a mixed technical/non-technical audience.
3. Given a full scenario, synthesize decisions across structure, rendering, data, state, and shared platform into one coherent, trade-off-justified proposal.

An architecture that lives only in your head is not an architecture — it's a hunch that happens to compile. The deliverable that actually makes you a staff-level architect isn't the diagram in a slide deck; it's a documented decision that a new hire can read in twenty minutes and understand not just what was chosen, but why, and what was deliberately rejected. This section is where every competency from Sections 1–6 converges into that single artifact.

terms.definition: a short, structured document capturing one architectural decision, its context, the alternatives considered, and the reasoning for the final choice.
a proposal document circulated for team feedback before a decision is finalized, often used for larger or more contested architectural changes.
the explicit line marking what is owned/controlled by one team or module versus another.
the explicit indication, in a diagram, of which way information moves between components (e.g., which system is the source of truth, which is a consumer).
the act of weighing multiple competing architectural forces against a specific context to reach and justify one decision.

contentBlocks.content:
## Documentation is not a summary written after the fact
The misconception to retire first: documentation is a summary written after the decision is made. A summary tells a reader what you chose. An effective ADR tells them what you didn't choose, and why — and this is where most of an ADR's future value lives. Six months from now, when someone proposes revisiting a decision, the value isn't re-explaining the chosen option; it's being able to say 'we considered X, and rejected it because of Y, which is still true' — or realizing Y is no longer true, and the decision should be revisited. Without the rejected-alternatives section, every ADR degrades into an unfalsifiable 'trust us' document.

## Anatomy of an effective ADR
A working structure, deliberately short enough that people actually write and read them:
- Title & status (proposed / accepted / superseded).
- Context: the requirements and constraints (this is where Section 1's elicitation work becomes visible in the artifact) that make this decision necessary now.
- Decision: the specific choice, stated plainly.
- Alternatives considered and rejected: each alternative, with one to two sentences on why it was rejected — specific to this context, not a generic statement of the alternative's general weaknesses.
- Consequences: what this decision makes easier, what it makes harder, and what future decisions it constrains.

## Diagrams that actually communicate, not just illustrate
The second misconception: a diagram is self-explanatory. A box-and-arrow diagram without explicit system boundaries (who owns what), explicit data-flow direction (which way information moves, and which system is the source of truth), and a short accompanying narrative creates the illusion of alignment while different readers silently interpret it differently. A useful discipline: every diagram should be able to answer, at a glance, 'if this breaks, whose pager goes off' and 'if I change this box, whose review do I need' — if it can't, the boundaries aren't explicit enough yet.

## The capstone synthesis: bringing every competency together
A full architecture proposal for a real scenario needs to visibly draw on every prior section, in the following practical sequence:
1. Elicit and categorize requirements (Section 1) — functional and non-functional, identifying which are decision-critical.
2. Choose a structural style and, if applicable, composition strategy (Section 2), justified against team topology now and 12–18 months out.
3. Assign rendering strategy per route and design the data-access layer (Section 3), justified against the SEO/freshness/personalization needs surfaced in step 1.
4. Design the state architecture (Section 4), distinguishing client/UI from server-cache state and resolving cross-module sharing if step 2 chose micro-frontends.
5. Define the shared platform layer (Section 5) — design system structure, governance, and which cross-cutting concerns are centralized.
6. Set and trace performance budgets and cross-cutting operational concerns (Section 6) back to the structural and rendering choices made in steps 2–3.
7. Write the ADR and diagram (this section) — documenting the decision, alternatives rejected at each step, and the consequences.

## Trade-off synthesis is the actual skill being tested
The final misconception to name directly, because it undercuts everything else if unaddressed: there is no single 'best practice' architecture that applies regardless of context, and more technology/flexibility is not always safer — optionality (extra composition mechanisms, extra state-sharing layers, extra abstraction) has a real ongoing cost in complexity and cognitive load that must be weighed against the flexibility it buys. The mark of a senior architect is not knowing the most patterns — it's correctly matching a small number of well-understood patterns to a specific context's actual constraints, and being able to say precisely why a fashionable alternative was rejected for this case.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
- **Common error 1:** Writing an ADR that only documents the chosen option. Without documented, context-specific rejection reasoning for the alternatives, the ADR can't be evaluated or revisited later — it becomes an assertion, not a record of reasoning.
- **Common error 2:** Producing a diagram with boxes and arrows but no ownership or data-flow-direction labels. This creates false alignment: two readers can walk away with different mental models of who owns what.
- **Common error 3:** Defaulting to more flexible/general architecture 'to be safe.' Extra optionality has a real, ongoing complexity cost; the safer choice is usually the one that most precisely matches the actual, current, evidenced constraints — not the one with the most future options built in.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which of the following best distinguishes an effective ADR from a simple summary of a decision?
options: An effective ADR uses more diagrams than a summary
An effective ADR documents the alternatives considered and the specific, context-based reasons each was rejected
An effective ADR is always longer than a summary
An effective ADR avoids discussing anything that was not ultimately chosen

optionFeedback.feedback: Diagram count isn't the distinguishing factor identified in the lecture; the content of the reasoning is.
Correct - matches the lecture's core point that most of an ADR's future value lives in the rejected-alternatives section.
Length isn't the criterion; a summary could be long and still lack rejection reasoning, or an ADR could be short and complete.
This directly contradicts the lecture's central point; omitting rejected alternatives is exactly the failure mode being warned against.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Six months from now, the value of an ADR isn't re-explaining what was chosen — it's being able to say 'we considered X and rejected it because of Y, which is still true' (or isn't). That's only possible if the alternatives were documented in the first place.
feedback.correctiveFeedback: Check whether an ADR explains what wasn't chosen and why, not just what was chosen.

workedExamples.problem: A B2B SaaS company's marketing site needs to move off pure CSR because organic search traffic (a stated NFR from their Section-1-style elicitation) is underperforming competitors. Write an ADR for the rendering-strategy decision.
steps: Decision: Adopt SSG for the marketing site, with ISR for the blog/case-studies section (content updates a few times a week), keeping the authenticated app dashboard as CSR.

Alternative 1 - Full SSR for everything: rejected because the marketing site's content changes rarely enough that paying a per-request server cost for pages that could be pre-rendered once is unjustified; would have also added infrastructure complexity disproportionate to the actual freshness need.

Alternative 2 - Leave everything as CSR and rely on client-side-rendering-aware crawling: rejected because too much risk given the explicit, measured underperformance in organic search already observed; the SEO NFR is a hard constraint, not a nice-to-have.

Alternative 3 - Full site migration to SSG, including the dashboard: rejected because the dashboard is authenticated, personalized, and not indexable by search engines in the first place, so pre-rendering it offers no SEO benefit and would force unnecessary rebuild-on-every-change complexity for user-specific data.

Consequences: content authors get a documented publish-to-live latency (ISR regeneration window) they need to be told about; the marketing team gains fast, cheap, reliably indexable pages; a future decision to add personalization to marketing pages would need to revisit this ADR, since SSG doesn't support per-user personalization without additional architecture.
workedExamples.conclusion: Notice that every rejected alternative is justified by this company's specific context (their SEO underperformance, their content update cadence, their dashboard's auth requirement) — not by a generic claim like 'SSR is slower.' This is what separates a defensible ADR from a preference statement.

fadedVariant.problem: A subscription cooking site's recipe pages currently use SSR on origin servers. Hosting costs are climbing, 95% of traffic is anonymous, organic search remains business-critical, and recipes rarely change after publication. Write the ADR for moving recipe pages to SSG with incremental revalidation.
givenSteps: Context section: state the NFRs driving reconsideration — cost pressure from per-request rendering, overwhelmingly anonymous cacheable traffic, SEO still a hard requirement, low post-publication change rate.
blankedStepPrompts: Write the decision statement in one sentence.
Write two 'alternatives considered and rejected' entries, each with a context-specific reason.
Write the consequences section, including at least one honestly accepted downside.
blankedStepAnswers: Recipe pages move to static generation with incremental revalidation triggered on publish/edit events; personalized elements (saved-recipe state) hydrate client-side after load.

Remain on SSR — rejected: it re-renders identical HTML for 95% anonymous traffic, which is precisely the cost line driving this decision. Move to pure CSR — rejected: organic search is a stated hard NFR and recipe pages are the primary landing surface; client rendering puts that traffic at risk.

Origin cost drops and TTFB improves via CDN-served static pages. Accepted downsides: edits appear only after revalidation completes (minutes-level staleness the team accepts for recipe content), and the publishing pipeline gains a dependency on the revalidation hook that must be monitored.

contentBlocks.title: Why this matters
contentBlocks.content: This workshop asks you to write a real ADR for the single highest-stakes decision you've made across the airline scenario in Sections 1–6. This is deliberately narrower than the full capstone proposal that follows — the goal here is depth on one decision, written the way it would actually need to be defended to a skeptical colleague six months from now.

selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: The regional airline booking platform scenario, spanning every decision made across Sections 1–6: requirements, structure/composition, rendering/data, state, shared platform, and performance/cross-cutting concerns.

instructions: Select the single decision from your work across Sections 2, 3, 4, or 5 that you consider highest-stakes for this airline platform, and briefly justify why you selected it over the others.
Write the Context section: the specific requirements and constraints from Section 1's elicitation that make this decision necessary.
Write the Decision section: state your choice plainly.

Write the Alternatives Considered and Rejected section: name at least two alternatives you didn't choose, and for each, write one to two sentences of rejection reasoning specific to this airline's facts — not a generic claim about the alternative.
Write the Consequences section: what this decision makes easier, what it makes harder, and what future decision it constrains.
Self-check: reread your rejection reasoning and confirm it couldn't be copy-pasted unchanged into an ADR for a completely different company. If it could, it's too generic.

Your prior decisions and reasoning from Sections 1 through 6 for the airline scenario

learningExperiences.title: Capstone: Full Architecture Proposal — Regional Grocery Delivery Startup

contentBlocks.title: Why this matters
contentBlocks.content: This is the final deliverable of the course, and deliberately uses a scenario you haven't seen before — a regional grocery delivery startup — rather than extending the airline scenario further. A staff architect's real value isn't reciting a memorized answer for one familiar company; it's applying the same seven-step synthesis sequence to a genuinely new context and reaching a defensible, context-specific conclusion.

selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: A regional grocery delivery startup: 20 engineers on one team today, planning to split into 3 teams within a year (likely along the lines of store-browsing/ordering, delivery logistics/tracking, and account/loyalty), moderate SEO dependency for store-locator pages, personalized order-tracking for logged-in users, and strict uptime needs during peak delivery windows.
selfGuidedExercise.objective: Produce a complete architecture proposal following the seven-step synthesis sequence from this section, culminating in one full ADR and a labeled diagram description.
instructions: Step 1 - Requirements: write a short requirements summary (functional and non-functional), flagging which non-functional requirements are decision-critical.
Step 2 - Structure: propose a structural/composition decision, justified against the team's timeline (1 team today, 3 teams within a year) rather than today's structure alone.

Step 3 - Rendering & data: produce a per-route rendering-strategy table (at minimum: store-locator pages, order-tracking dashboard) and a data-access layer design (BFF, GraphQL, or both), each justified against the requirements from Step 1.
Step 4 - State: propose a state-architecture plan, distinguishing client/UI from server-cache state, and specify a cross-module state-sharing approach if Step 2 chose a decomposed structure.
Step 5 - Shared platform: propose a design-system layering approach, a governance model sized to this team's timeline, and name which cross-cutting concerns you'd centralize.
Step 6 - Performance: propose two concrete performance budgets (e.g., a JS payload limit and an LCP target for a specific route), and trace each back to a specific decision made in Steps 2–3.

Step 7 - Document: write one full ADR (using the five-part structure) for the single decision you consider highest-stakes in this proposal, and write a short labeled-diagram description (boundaries, ownership, data-flow direction) for the overall system.

Final check: for at least one major decision, explicitly state which plausible alternative you rejected and why, using reasoning specific to this grocery-delivery scenario rather than a general architectural preference.
materialsOrPrerequisites: Completion of all prior sections in this course
A document or notes app to record your full proposal, since this exercise produces a multi-part deliverable
reflectionPrompts: Which step of the seven-step sequence took the most iteration before you were confident in your answer?
Did any decision from an earlier step force you to revisit a decision from a step before it? Which, and why?
If you had to defend this proposal to a skeptical VP in five minutes, which single piece of evidence from your requirements (Step 1) would you lead with?

selfAssessmentCriteria: My proposal visibly completes all seven steps, in order, each building on the ones before it
Every major decision is justified by a specific fact from this scenario, not a generic architectural preference
My ADR includes context-specific rejection reasoning for at least two alternatives
My diagram description explicitly specifies ownership and data-flow direction, not just boxes and arrows
I explicitly rejected at least one plausible alternative for my structural decision, with scenario-specific reasoning

sectionSummary.content: Architecture documentation is written at decision time, not summarized after the fact — its audience is the future reader who wasn't in the room. An effective ADR pairs context (the constraints that actually drove the choice) with a decision, honestly rejected alternatives, and consequences including accepted downsides. Diagrams earn their place when they communicate a specific decision, not when they merely illustrate. The capstone sequence is the whole course in miniature: elicit constraints, choose structure, assign rendering and state strategies, plan the platform layer, set budgets, and document the trade-offs. The skill being tested throughout is trade-off synthesis — defending a choice by what it costs, given this context.
keyTakeaways: Document at decision time, for the future reader who lacks today's context
An ADR = context + decision + alternatives honestly rejected + consequences (including accepted downsides)
'Alternatives considered' carries the document's future value — it stops relitigation and flags invalidated context
Diagrams should communicate a decision, not decorate a document
Trade-off synthesis — naming what your choice costs and why that's acceptable here — is the capstone skill

sections.title: CSS and Motion: Letting the Platform Do the Work
sections.description: One habit costs more performance for less benefit than any other in this course: solving in JavaScript what the browser already solves in CSS. This section gives you a decision rule for when to reach for the platform and when JavaScript is genuinely needed, then applies it to three areas — layout response (where container queries remove the variant prop Section 3 argued against), cascade structure (layers, tokens, logical properties), and motion (which tools to use, and why a reduced-motion response is not a switch). Examples come from a museum's public collections website.

learningObjectives.description: Apply the CSS-or-JavaScript decision rule to hover, focus, sticky positioning, and data-driven styling, and justify each assignment.
Explain why a platform implementation is frequently more correct, not only faster, by naming an input mode a JavaScript reimplementation commonly misses.
Replace a viewport-driven layout variant prop with a container query, removing the prop entirely and verifying the component in more than one context.
Resolve a specificity conflict by declaring cascade layer order rather than escalating specificity or using `!important`.
Implement theming with custom properties and confirm with the profiler that switching causes zero React renders.
Adopt logical properties by default and state the cost asymmetry between doing so now and retrofitting them later.
Choose the correct motion tool in order of preference, and justify installing an animation library only by React's node-removal behaviour rather than by animation in general.
Design a reduced-motion response that removes travel while preserving the signal that something changed.

motivationHooks.prompt: A museum's collections grid used three `useState` hooks per card — for hover, focus, and a reveal — across sixty visible cards. That is 180 hooks, and 38 to 44 milliseconds of scripting every time a pointer crossed the grid. Nobody had measured it, because it did not look like a performance problem; it looked like ordinary React code. It was also invisible to the site's accessibility audit, because the audit checked whether elements had labels, not whether a keyboard user could ever reach them. Both defects were removed by deleting code, not by writing more.

Write this down before reading on. A card should show a shadow on hover. A developer implements it with `useState` and `onMouseEnter`/`onMouseLeave`. It works perfectly in every manual test. **Name one real user for whom this implementation is completely broken** — not slow, not awkward, but unable to see the shadow at all. You do not need to know CSS to answer this; you need to know who uses a mouse and who does not.

This section finishes an argument Section 3 started. There, a `variant` prop chosen from viewport width was shown to break in a sidebar, because it asked the wrong question. Container queries here are the fix — they let the component answer the right question itself, and the prop disappears. The same 'ask the platform first' instinct then extends to motion: before Section 9 teaches you to measure performance, this section removes an entire category of performance problem by never creating it.

The user is anyone navigating by keyboard. `onMouseEnter` and `onMouseLeave` are pointer events — they never fire from Tab, from a screen reader's virtual cursor, or from switch-access hardware. So a keyboard user does not see the shadow late or clumsily; they never see it, and if the shadow reveals content rather than merely decorating the card, that content simply does not exist for them. `:hover, :focus-within` in two lines of CSS covers both groups. Hold onto the shape of this answer — 'the platform version is not just faster, it is more correct' — because it recurs through the whole section.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following about styling and motion in a React application.

**If the browser can express a behaviour declaratively, let it.** The test is concrete: ask what information the behaviour needs that the browser does not already have. Hover, focus, sticky positioning, and layout response to available space all fail that test — the browser already has everything it needs, and JavaScript reimplementations of them cost renders and commonly break for keyboard users.

**Container queries answer a question media queries cannot.** A component's real constraint is the space it was given, not the width of the screen, and a `variant` prop chosen from viewport width breaks the moment someone places the component somewhere new. This closes Section 3's argument about props expressing meaning rather than presentation.

**Cascade layers replace the specificity arms race.** Layer order beats specificity outright, so a single-class utility can override a deeply nested component rule with no `!important` anywhere.

**Custom properties are runtime values.** Changing one re-themes the application with zero React renders, which is Section 1's reference-equality rule appearing in CSS: the DOM updates without React's tree ever being asked to compare anything.

**Logical properties cost nothing today and save a great deal later.** In a left-to-right interface they behave exactly like physical properties; the saving only appears the day right-to-left support is needed, and by then it is too late to have made the decision cheaply.

**Motion explains change; it does not decorate it.** Prefer transitions, then keyframes, then the Web Animations API, then a library — and the one genuinely React-specific reason for a library is that React removes a node before CSS can animate its exit.

**Reduced motion means removing travel, not removing feedback.** A blunt global switch stops harm today; a considered per-animation pass restores communication afterwards. Both matter, in that order.
keyTakeaways: Test: what does this need that the browser doesn't already have? If nothing, use CSS.
The platform version is frequently more correct, not only faster — it is what covers keyboard, touch, and assistive technology by default.
Container queries let a component answer 'how much space do I have' itself, removing variant props from component APIs.
@layer beats specificity; declare an order once instead of escalating forever.
Custom properties re-theme with zero React renders.
Adopt logical properties now — the cost is zero today and large on retrofit.
Animate transform and opacity; they can run on the compositor without recalculating layout.
The only React-specific justification for an animation library is animating an element's removal.
Reduced motion: remove the travel, keep the state-change signal.

learningExperiences.title: The decision rule: what does the browser already have?

contentBlocks.content:
## The habit, and its cost

React makes state feel free, so implementing a hover effect with `useState` looks entirely reasonable. It costs an event listener, a state update, a render, and a commit — every time a pointer crosses the element — to reproduce something `:hover` does with no JavaScript at all, on a code path the browser has optimised for two decades.

**Your JavaScript runs on the main thread. Much of what CSS does runs in the browser's own engine, and transform and opacity animation, plus scrolling, can run off the main thread entirely.**

## The test

**If the browser can express the behaviour declaratively, let it. Reach for JavaScript when you need information or sequencing the browser does not have.**

Ask one question: *what does this need that the browser doesn't already have?* If the answer is "nothing," you are about to reimplement a selector.

contentBlocks.caption: Common React-state patterns and their platform equivalents
rows: Style a parent by its content

contentBlocks.content:
## Not just faster — more correct

The hover row deserves emphasis, because the argument for it is not only about performance.

`onMouseEnter` never fires for keyboard users. So the JavaScript version does not merely animate more slowly for them — it silently withholds the content entirely. `:hover, :focus-within` covers both pointer and keyboard input in two selectors.

This pattern repeats. `resize` listeners produce a wrong first paint before the first measurement runs, so users on a slow connection briefly see the wrong layout. `scroll` listeners for sticky headers run on the main thread during scrolling, which is precisely when the main thread is busiest and least able to spare the time — so the hand-written version janks worst on the low-powered devices that most need it to be smooth.

**When JavaScript genuinely is the right tool:** the style depends on data you fetched; you need measurement the browser does not expose declaratively, such as a tooltip flipping before it overflows the viewport; you need to animate an element that is being removed from the DOM (the next experience returns to this); or you need gesture handling or spring physics.

interactionSequence.prompt: A reveal-on-hover implemented with `useState` and `onMouseEnter` passes an automated accessibility scan with zero violations. What has the scan not detected?
options: The revealed content lacks an accessible name
The content is unreachable for keyboard users, because `onMouseEnter` never fires without a pointer
The revealed text has insufficient colour contrast
There is no undetected problem; the scan result is correct

optionFeedback.feedback: A missing accessible name is exactly the kind of static markup defect automated tools are good at finding. The gap here is behavioural, not structural — the markup itself can be perfectly valid.

Correct, and it is invisible to scanners precisely because the markup is valid. The content exists in the DOM; it simply never becomes visible without a mouse. `:hover, :focus-within` closes the gap in two selectors.
Contrast is one of the things automated tools check reliably. It is not what a pointer-only implementation causes.

A clean scan means no detectable violations, not that the interface is operable by every input method. Automated tools find roughly a third of real accessibility problems — a figure Section 9 returns to.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Keep this example in mind for Section 9, where the same shape of defect — content technically present, practically unreachable — is what a virtualized grid does to keyboard navigation when it is built without deliberate design. The pattern is the same: something that looks fine to an automated check and fails completely for a real keyboard user.
hints: Does `onMouseEnter` fire when an element receives focus via Tab?

interactionSequence.prompt: A filter bar must stay pinned to the top of the collections grid while the page scrolls. A developer implements this with a `scroll` event listener that toggles a `.pinned` class. On a museum-provided iPad in the galleries, scrolling is visibly rough. What is the fix, and why does it matter more on that device than on a developer's laptop?
options: Use `position: sticky`, which the browser can handle without running a listener on the main thread during every scroll frame
Debounce the scroll listener so it runs less often
Move the listener into a Web Worker
Reduce the number of cards rendered in the grid

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. `position: sticky` is handled by the browser's compositor, not by a main-thread listener, so it holds frame rate under exactly the conditions — a busy main thread on modest hardware — where the hand-written version struggles most.

Debouncing reduces how often the listener runs but does not remove the fundamental cost: it is still main-thread work competing with everything else happening during a scroll, on a device with less main-thread budget to spare.

A Web Worker cannot touch the DOM directly, so it cannot toggle a class in response to scroll position without a round trip back to the main thread — which reintroduces the cost this approach is trying to avoid.
Fewer cards would help overall render cost, but it does not address the specific mechanism causing scroll jank, which is the scroll listener itself running on the main thread.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The device detail is the point worth keeping. A scroll listener that feels acceptable on a developer's laptop can be unusable on the actual hardware visitors use, because the two devices have very different amounts of spare main-thread capacity. `position: sticky` sidesteps the question entirely by not needing any.
hints: What thread does a `scroll` event handler run on, and what else is competing for that thread during a scroll?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: think of one place in a codebase you know where interaction styling — hover, focus, or a pressed state — is implemented with React state. What would you check to find out whether it is a real problem, and what would you look for specifically for keyboard users?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong answer names two separate checks rather than one. For the performance question: profile a pointer traverse across a realistic number of instances with CPU throttling enabled, and look at scripting time. For the correctness question: unplug the mouse, or simply stop using it, and tab through the same interface — if content that a sighted mouse user sees never appears, that is not a performance defect at all, it is a content-access defect, and it will not show up in any profiler.

steps: Identify what Version A costs on interaction. Each `onMouseEnter`/`onMouseLeave` pair triggers a state update, which triggers a render of `ObjectCard`, which produces a new description for reconciliation to compare. Across sixty visible cards and a pointer moving through the grid, that is a render per card boundary crossed.

Identify what Version A costs structurally. `{hovered &&

...}` conditionally mounts and unmounts the accession-number paragraph. Because it never exists in the DOM until hovered, it is unreachable by any means that does not fire `onMouseEnter` — which, per this experience, excludes every keyboard user.
Compare the render cost. Version B has no state, so hovering never triggers a React render at all — the browser handles the entire interaction in its own style-recalculation pipeline.

Compare what each version actually delivers to a keyboard user. In Version A, tabbing to a link inside the card never sets `hovered`, so the accession number never appears — the content does not exist for that user. In Version B, `:focus-within` matches when any descendant receives focus, so the same reveal happens for keyboard navigation with no additional code.

Note one real trade-off, not a false equivalence. In Version B, the accession number is always present in the DOM and always announced by screen readers, even when visually hidden by opacity. This is usually correct for supplementary text, but it is a decision, not an accident — opacity hides *visually*, not *semantically*. If the content should be genuinely absent until revealed, use `display: none` or keep the conditional render, and accept the keyboard cost consciously rather than by default.

State the conclusion in testable form: profile Version A across sixty cards with a pointer traverse and record the scripting time; then tab through both versions and record which one shows the accession number.
workedExamples.conclusion: Version B is shorter, has no state, and never renders on hover. But the render-cost argument is not even the strongest one here — the keyboard argument is. A performance review of Version A would find a real but survivable cost; a keyboard-only walkthrough of Version A finds content that a significant group of users can never reach at all. When platform and JavaScript implementations of the same behaviour differ, check correctness before you check speed, because the correctness gap is usually the bigger and less forgivable one.

Name three behaviours commonly implemented with React state that are platform features, and for one of them, state a cost beyond performance.
